target.title: RESOUND: Speech Reconstruction from Silent Videos via Acoustic-Semantic Decomposed Modeling
target.venue: arXiv preprint [cs.SD] (no proceedings venue stated on first page)

entries.text: Novelty claim: RESOUND is the first L2S study to incorporate source-filter theory.
entries.condition: Authors' literature-priority claim; the paper offers no systematic novelty search protocol.
entries.quote: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to incorporate source-filter theory into L2S synthesis.

entries.text: The proposed source-filter-inspired architecture separates an acoustic prosody path from a semantic linguistic path for independent learning.
entries.condition: Silent talking-face video plus a brief speaker audio prompt; acoustic path models prosody/timbre and semantic path uses visual features and L2T predictions.

entries.text: The decoder predicts mel-spectrograms and discrete speech units for a multi-input vocoder, which authors say preserves content and speaker identity while adding expressiveness.
entries.condition: The mel and unit representations are both passed toward waveform synthesis; speech units are described as an unsupervised representation.

entries.text: Authors claim RESOUND consistently outperforms prior L2S models across multiple metrics; their own results show this varies by dataset and metric.
entries.condition: Comparative results are reported on LRS3-TED and LRS2-BBC; see Table 1 row entries and the explicit LRS2 WER exception.

entries.text: On LRS2, authors claim improvement over prior SOTA approaches across multiple metrics except WER; LipVoicer has lower WER in Table 1.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC test set; Table 1 reports RESOUND WER 28.55 and LipVoicer WER 17.04 (table unit not stated).

entries.text: Authors attribute the LRS2 WER shortfall to unpredictable dataset noise and say this hinders accurate reconstruction.
entries.condition: Author explanation for LRS2 results; no noise-stratified analysis or causal test is reported.
entries.quote:
This discrepancy can be explained by the unpre-
dictable noise present in LRS2

entries.text: Authors leave adaptability to diverse languages and accents as future work; experiments reported here use English corpora.
entries.condition: Future-work statement; no non-English or accent-stratified experiment is reported.

entries.text: LRS2-BBC is described as over 220 hours; pretraining and training sets are used for development and test set for inference.
entries.condition: English BBC audio-visual dataset; paper gives no test utterance count, test-speaker count, speaker-overlap analysis, or session split.

entries.text: LRS3-TED is described as 438 hours with a 50,000+ word vocabulary; the paper says it trains on 131,000 utterances and tests on around 1,300.
entries.unit: hours of video; words; training utterances; test utterances
entries.condition: English TED/TEDx dataset with diverse speakers; test speaker count, train-test speaker overlap, exact test count, and test vocabulary are not specified.
entries.quote: Following [27], we train on 131,000 and test on around 1,300 utterances.

entries.text: Reported training duration is 80 epochs (40k steps per dataset) with initial learning rate 10^-3.
entries.unit: epochs; optimization steps per dataset; learning rate
entries.condition: Reported for the model across datasets; no training seed, number of repeats, or validation/checkpoint selection protocol is stated in the paper.

entries.text: The Conformer has eight layers; each branch generator has three FFT blocks with hidden dimension 512 and eight attention heads; Mel-Decoder is a 1D CNN.
entries.unit: layers; blocks; hidden dimensions; attention heads; CNN dimensionality
entries.condition: Architecture implementation details; training dataset and model configuration are those described in Sec. 3.

entries.text: Total loss weights are mel 100, pitch 0.1, energy 0.1, and units 0.01; unit-loss label smoothing is 0.1.
entries.condition: Training objective for RESOUND; L1 reconstruction losses for mel, pitch, and energy, cross-entropy for speech units.

entries.text: MediaPipe mouth ROI is 96×96 pixels with random 88×88 crops; augmentation also includes flipping, erasing, and temporal masking.
entries.condition: Visual preprocessing in the reported implementation.

entries.text: Audio is resampled to 16 kHz; HuBERT-BASE with 200 K-means clusters supplies speech units; a random 0.5 s ground-truth audio segment is used as prompt.
entries.condition: Audio preprocessing and prompt construction described in implementation details; the paper does not state the test-time prompt-selection protocol.
entries.quote: Following [11], we randomly extract a 0.5s segment from the ground-truth audio to serve as an audio prompt.

entries.text: Evaluation uses UTMOS for naturalness, SECS for speaker similarity, Auto-AVSR-derived WER for intelligibility, MAEF0/MAERMSE for prosody, ESTOI for intelligibility, MCD-DTW-SL for acoustic distance, and RTF for speed.
entries.condition: SECS is computed via Resemblyzer; paper omits metric-unit definitions, Auto-AVSR checkpoint/decoding and text normalization, and RTF hardware/runtime settings.

entries.text: MOS study: 30 participants rated 20 randomly synthesized samples per method from LRS3-TED on a 5-point scale in 0.5-point increments; Table 2 gives 95% confidence intervals.
entries.unit: participants; samples per method; rating-scale points; point increments; percent confidence interval
entries.condition: Subjective MOS test on LRS3-TED; rater demographics, assignment/order, sample-level protocol, and CI computation are not reported.
entries.quote:
In this evaluation, 30 participants rate the quality of 20 ran-
domly synthesized audio samples per method on a 5-point scale
with 0.5-point increments.

entries.text: Ablation narrative reports a 37% relative WER increase without L2T and SRA, and relative degradations of 28% in naturalness and 40% in pitch error without the acoustic branch.
entries.unit: percent relative increase; percent relative degradation; percent relative degradation
entries.condition: Ablation experiments on LRS3-TED; Table 3 reports one set of values but no repeated-run or significance protocol.

This separated structure leads to the improvement of speech ac-

entries.text: Frozen AV-HuBERT visual embeddings feed FFT-based content and pitch generators: content is supervised by SSL speech units and yields embeddings Z; the pitch path combines upsampled visual features with Z to predict coarse log-F0, an auxiliary mel, then refined log-F0 for DDSP.
entries.condition: Architecture; experiments use LRS2/LRS3 original splits, multi-speaker and unconstrained-vocabulary data; decoding/LM and seeds not stated.

entries.text: Refined predicted F0 is interpolated to sample rate to set sinusoid phase; ConvReLUNorm predicts amplitudes and harmonic weights for the periodic voiced component yh.
entries.condition: Architecture; experiments use LRS2/LRS3 original splits, multi-speaker and unconstrained-vocabulary data; decoding/LM and seeds not stated.

entries.text: The noise branch is conditioned on content embedding Z and predicts an aperiodic amplitude spectrogram, combined with uniform-noise phase and iSTFT; DDSP sums this component with the harmonic signal.
entries.condition: Architecture; experiments use LRS2/LRS3 original splits, multi-speaker and unconstrained-vocabulary data; decoding/LM and seeds not stated.

entries.text: Conditional HiFi-GAN takes content Z and coarse DSP waveform ydsp instead of a mel-spectrogram; downsampled DSP features are concatenated with upsampled features at each block/MRF to generate the final waveform.
entries.condition: Architecture; experiments use LRS2/LRS3 original splits, multi-speaker and unconstrained-vocabulary data; decoding/LM and seeds not stated.

entries.text: NaturalL2S frames DDSP as an acoustic inductive bias and describes a harmonic-plus-noise decomposition, not explicitly as source-filter theory. Unlike RESOUND's excitation/formant branches, its stated DDSP split is periodic harmonic versus aperiodic noise, with no separate formant branch described.
entries.condition: Architecture description; no test-set, speaker, vocabulary, decoding/LM, or seed condition applies.

entries.text: Full-model runtime covers the V2S frontend and vocoder. Compare RTF with RESOUND only after including its prompt-path cost and matching test-time input handling; this paper reports no RTF.
entries.condition: DiVISe full model is frontend plus vocoder; align the RESOUND prompt path and both papers' test-time protocols before deriving a relative RTF.

entries.text: The visual frontend uses pre-trained AV-HuBERT (modified ResNet-18 plus a 12-layer, 1024-dimensional, 16-head Transformer), followed by four Conformer blocks with 256-dimensional attention and four heads; linear upsampling/projection aligns it to mel frames.
entries.condition: Visual-only silent-video input; model architecture in Sec. 4.1.

entries.text: The decoder predicts explicit Mel-spectrograms, not discrete speech units; the paper describes no separate prosody prediction stream.
entries.condition: V2S frontend maps video frames to mel features; the predicted mels are trained against ground-truth mels.

entries.text: HiFi-GAN is the downstream neural vocoder that converts the predicted Mel-spectrogram into an audio waveform.
entries.condition: Vocoder is pretrained on audio-only LJSpeech and fine-tuned for the generated-mel distribution.

entries.text: Full-resource DiVISe on LRS3-TED reports PESQ 1.17, STOI 0.527, ESTOI 0.331, and WER 35.68%.

entries.text: The paper cautions that its ASR setting may not match the settings used for other methods, limiting direct WER comparisons.
entries.condition: Table 2 WER comparison across methods.

entries.text: The L2T model that supplies text predictions to the semantic branch is reference [22], Auto-AVSR (Ma et al.); its text is converted to phonemes by a G2P model.
entries.quote: we integrate an advanced L2T model [22] to generate textual predictions.

entries.text: Prosody (pitch, energy, timbre) is estimated from a brief speaker prompt.
entries.quote: Prosody is estimated from a brief speaker prompt using pitch, energy, and timbre to capture speaker-specific characteristics

entries.text: Semantic Reference Attention (SRA) fuses visual features with phoneme embeddings from the L2T text.
The Spec-Ling decoder has an Excitation Generator (source) and a Formant Generator (filter) whose outputs are added to form a coarse mel-spectrogram.
entries.quote: These two representations are combined using a simple additive fusion method to form a coarse mel-spectrogram

entries.text: The authors credit FastPitchFormant [17] (TTS) with pioneering source-filter neural acoustic modeling.
The authors note that [13] (Hegde et al., 2023) already incorporates L2T models.
The acoustic-branch ablation removes both the Prosody Encoder and the Excitation Generator.
entries.quote: we remove both the Prosody Encoder and Excitation Generator.

entries.text: The authors read the L2T-and-SRA ablation as support for disentangled linguistic and acoustic branches: WER rises 37% relative while quality stays largely unaffected.

questions.q: What does RESOUND claim is novel, and what are its two main modeling paths?
questions.answer: It claims to be the first L2S system to incorporate source-filter theory; the acoustic path models prompt-conditioned prosody/timbre, while the semantic path combines visual cues with L2T-derived linguistic features. Speech units and mel-spectrograms jointly condition waveform synthesis.

questions.q: What are the main comparative results, and where does the superiority claim have an explicit exception?
questions.answer: Table 1 reports all dataset/model metric rows in t18–t31. The authors explicitly acknowledge that RESOUND does not lead WER on LRS2: 28.55 versus LipVoicer at 17.04; they attribute the discrepancy to LRS2 noise.

questions.q: What were the subjective MOS results and the reported rating protocol?
questions.answer: Thirty participants rated 20 randomly synthesized LRS3-TED samples per method on a 5-point scale with half-point increments. Table 2 reports three MOS dimensions and 95% confidence intervals for Ground Truth, DiffV2S, Intelligible L2S, LipVoicer, and RESOUND.

questions.q: What evaluation conditions are missing from the paper?
questions.answer: The paper omits exact split/speaker/session details, training seeds and repetitions, validation/checkpoint selection, normalization, chance levels, WER normalization/decoding and LM details, MOS rater/protocol details, baseline harmonization, and RTF hardware/timing settings.

questions.q: What does the public repository add about training and decoding?
questions.answer: The configs set AV-HuBERT seed 1337 and vocoder seed 1234, identify train/valid subsets and a validation checkpoint metric, enable normalization, and configure test decoding with no external LM. The example LRS3 inference path is label_eval_in_train, so it should not be assumed to be the reported Table 1 test run.

questions.q: What limitations or caveats do the authors themselves identify?
questions.answer: They attribute LRS2 WER weakness to unpredictable noise, omit LSE-* because some methods outperform ground truth and impair synchronization reliability, and leave adaptability to diverse languages and accents for future work.

questions.q: Writer: what is L2T and SRA, where does the test-time prompt come from, what are the excitation/formant branches, what does the acoustic-branch ablation remove, and does RTF include L2T? (free model failed; answered from targeted passages of the source text)
questions.answer: L2T is Auto-AVSR [22] text converted by G2P; SRA is Semantic Reference Attention; excitation and formant generators are added into a coarse mel; the acoustic ablation removes the Prosody Encoder and Excitation Generator; the prompt is a random 0.5 s ground-truth segment, test-time source not stated; RTF scope and hardware not stated.
